nodes.title: Unramified descent for torus torsors
nodes.statement: Let k be a number field, X smooth geometrically integral and f : Y → X a torsor under a k-torus T. Put A = f*^{-1}(Br_nr(Y)) ⊆ Br X. Then X(𝔸_k)^A ⊆ ⋃_{σ ∈ H¹(k,T)} f_σ(Y^σ(𝔸_k)^{Br_nr(Y^σ)}). If X is proper then A = Br X. No rational connectedness is assumed.
hypotheses: k a number field; X smooth geometrically integral; T a k-torus.
proofSteps: Lift (x_v) to some twist Y^σ(𝔸) (torus-descent-brauer, Harpaz–Wittenberg Proposition 2.5).
Choose σ in its Ш¹-coset so that ε_σ = 0 (residual-sha-functional and Poitou–Tate perfectness).

With ε_σ = 0, extend the evaluation functional through the edge image to H²(k, T̂); adelic torus duality supplies (t_v) with y_v ↦ t_v^{-1}y_v orthogonal to Br_nr(Y^σ) (Proposition 2.7, using edge-map-twist-independence (iv)).
acceptance: For T = 1 the statement is X(𝔸)^{Br_nr} ⊆ X(𝔸)^{Br_nr}.

sources.match: Adelic points orthogonal to the pulled-back unramified classes lift to Brauer–Manin points of some twist; A = Br X for proper X.

nodes.title: Descent from a torus torsor over a dense open subset
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth proper rationally connected variety over a number field k, V ⊆ X dense open and f : W → V a torsor under a k-torus. Then X(𝔸_k)^{Br X} is contained in the closure in X(𝔸_k) of ⋃_σ f_σ(W^σ(𝔸_k)^{Br_nr(W^σ)}). The input is that A = f*^{-1}Br_nr(W) ⊆ Br V has A/(A ∩ Br X) finite: after deleting a codimension ≥ 2 subset the compactified morphism is flat, and geometric codimension-one fibres have a multiplicity-one component.
hypotheses: X smooth proper rationally connected; V dense open; W → V a torus torsor.
proofSteps: Finite quotient A/Br X (Colliot-Thélène–Skorobogatov 2000, proof of Lemma 3.1, as invoked by Harpaz–Wittenberg).
Harari's formal lemma (RP.2/formal-lemma) gives density of V(𝔸)^A in X(𝔸)^{A ∩ Br X} ⊇ X(𝔸)^{Br X}; apply unramified-torus-descent on V (Harpaz–Wittenberg Corollary 2.2).
acceptance: For V=𝔸ⁿ⊂ℙⁿ and the trivial torus torsor V×𝔾_mⁿ→V, the conclusion specializes to density of the affine open in the proper adelic space. The coordinatewise inclusion 𝔾_mⁿ→𝔸ⁿ is not a torsor over 𝔸ⁿ.

sources.locator: Corollaire 2.2 and proof, p. 8, citing Colliot-Thélène–Skorobogatov 2000 Proposition 1.1 and the proof of Lemma 3.1
sources.match: Descent from an open torus torsor on a smooth proper rationally connected variety, via the finite ramification quotient and the formal lemma.

nodes.title: Brauer–Manin points give universal torsors
nodes.statement: For a smooth proper geometrically rationally connected variety X over a number field k, if X(𝔸_k)^{Br X} ≠ ∅ then a universal torsor over X exists over k. More generally, for a torus T' and a type λ : T̂' → Pic X_{k̄}, the obstruction to the existence of a torsor of type λ is detected by Br₁ X, and vanishes when X(𝔸)^{Br₁} ≠ ∅.
hypotheses: X smooth proper geometrically rationally connected (so k̄[X]^× = k̄^× and Pic X_{k̄} is free of finite rank).
proofSteps: The existence obstruction of a torsor of type λ lies in H²(k, T') and pairs with the adelic point through Br₁ X by Poitou–Tate (Colliot-Thélène–Sansuc; Skorobogatov 2001 Proposition 6.1.4, as invoked by Harpaz–Wittenberg §6–7).
acceptance: If X(k) ≠ ∅ the conclusion holds trivially.

sources.match: Brauer–Manin points imply existence over k of a universal torsor (citing Skorobogatov, Torsors and rational points, Proposition 6.1.4); the prescribed-type version through the type obstruction.

nodes.title: Genus-one curves as torsors and the Weil–Châtelet group
nodes.statement: Let E be an elliptic curve over a field k. A smooth projective genus-one curve C over k with Jacobian E is a torsor under E, and isomorphism classes of such torsors are in bijection with the Weil–Châtelet group WC(E/k) = H¹(k, E(k^s)) of TauCetiRoadmap EllipticCurves Layer 7; the trivial class corresponds to E, i.e. to C(k) ≠ ∅. Over a number field Ш(E/k) ⊆ WC(E/k) consists of the everywhere locally soluble C. This is a different classification from the pointed twists of EllipticCurves Layer 5 (H¹(k, Aut(E, O))): a pointed twist always has a rational point. The H¹(k,E) classification fixes an identification of the Jacobian with E and uses E-equivariant isomorphisms. Unmarked genus-one curves with Jacobian isomorphic to E require the further Aut(E)-orbit quotient.
hypotheses: k a field; E elliptic; C smooth projective of genus one with Pic⁰_C ≅ E.
proofSteps: C is an E-torsor through the action of Pic⁰ on Pic¹ ≅ C (SchemeAndStackFoundations SF.3/genus-one-curves); torsor classes are H¹(k, E) (SF.1/torsor-cohomology with Poonen Theorem 6.5.10).
A torsor is trivial iff it has a k-point (Poonen Proposition 5.12.14).
Comparison with Layer 5: the forgetful map from pointed twists to curves lands in the trivial torsor classes of the twisted Jacobians.
acceptance: The genus-one curve 2w² = x⁴ + 1 of Poonen §8.3 has the point (1, 1), so it is the trivial torsor under its Jacobian.

sources.locator: §5.12, Example 5.12.12 (genus-one curves as torsors under the Albanese/Jacobian) and Proposition 5.12.14, pp. 153–155
sources.match: A nice genus-one curve is a torsor under its Jacobian; a torsor is trivial iff it has a rational point.

sources.locator: TauCetiRoadmap EllipticCurves, Layer 7 (Weil–Châtelet group) and Layer 5 (pointed twists)
sources.match: WC(E/K) as cohomology, with its geometric reading assigned to the scheme-facing roadmap; pointed twists are a different theory.

nodes.title: Hasse principle failures for J¹ and Sym^k C with Brauer–Manin obstruction
nodes.statement: For hyperelliptic curves C : y² = f(x) over ℚ of genus g ≥ 1 (deg f = 2g + 2), ordered by height: for fixed g a positive proportion of everywhere locally soluble C have J¹(ℚ) = ∅ with a Brauer–Manin obstruction on the g-dimensional variety J¹ (Bhargava–Gross–Wang Theorem 10); for fixed odd k > 0 the proportion of locally soluble C for which Sym^k(C) fails the Hasse principle tends to 1 as g → ∞, and the failure is a Brauer–Manin obstruction (Corollary 9, Theorem 11).
hypotheses: Density statements for the family of locally soluble hyperelliptic curves ordered by the height of f.
proofSteps: Sel₂(J¹) = ∅ (RP.1/selmer-set-two-covering) gives a descent obstruction by the J[2]-torsor of two-coverings; for torsors under abelian varieties this descent obstruction is a Brauer–Manin obstruction (descent-brauer-comparison together with Manin's interpretation of Ш through Br₁).
The density statements are the averaging theorems of Bhargava–Gross–Wang, imported as stated.
acceptance: For g = 1, J¹ ≅ C and Theorem 10 gives a positive proportion of locally soluble genus-one curves with no rational point.

sources.match: Positive-proportion Hasse principle failures for J¹ and Sym^k(C), explained by the Brauer–Manin obstruction.

nodes.title: A worked descent: y² = (x² + 1)(x⁴ + 1)
nodes.statement: For the genus-two curve X : y² = (x² + 1)(x⁴ + 1) over ℚ, the μ₂-torsors Z_c → X given by c·w² = x⁴ + 1 (c ∈ ℚ^×/ℚ^{×2}) partition X(ℚ) (descent-partition); only c ∈ {1, 2} are everywhere locally soluble (the Selmer set); Z_c maps to the genus-one curves Y₁ : w² = x⁴ + 1 and Y₂ : 2w² = x⁴ + 1, birational respectively to the rank-zero elliptic curves y² = x³ − 4x and y² = x³ − x; hence X(ℚ) consists of the six affine points (0, ±1), (±1, ±2) and the two points at infinity. A rational point of X lifts to exactly one twist, and the other twists have no rational point although some are locally soluble at many places.
hypotheses: Torsors under μ₂ over the genus-two curve; the rank computations are 2-descents (RP.1/elliptic-two-descent-example for y² = x³ − x).
proofSteps: Resultant argument: only p = 2 divides both factors, so X⁴ + Z⁴ = c W² with c ∈ {±1, ±2}, positivity forces c ∈ {1, 2} (Poonen §8.3).
Rank zero and torsion ℤ/2 × ℤ/2 of both elliptic curves give the finite point sets.

Specify the elliptic labels rather than reading an ordering into Poonen’s unordered pair. For w²=x⁴+1, X=2(w+1)/x² and Y=4(w+1)/x³ give Y²=X³−4X. The twist 2w²=x⁴+1 has Jacobian isomorphic to Y²=X³−X. Extend the birational maps across the missing points on the smooth projective models.
acceptance: #X(ℚ) = 8 including the two rational points at infinity.

sources.match: The descent computation for y² = (x² + 1)(x⁴ + 1), reduction to the twists c ∈ {1, 2} and the six affine solutions.

nodes.title: Finite étale covers obstruct strong approximation
nodes.statement: Let k be a global field, S a finite set of places and f : Y → X a finite étale morphism of geometrically integral k-varieties that is not an isomorphism. If X(𝔸^S) ≠ ∅ then X(k) is not dense in X(𝔸^S). Consequently a normal geometrically integral variety with X(𝔸^S) ≠ ∅ and X_{k^s} not algebraically simply connected fails strong approximation off S.
hypotheses: k global; f finite étale of degree > 1; the adeles away from S.

For function fields the assertion requires the analogous adelic-space construction for global fields. RP.2 currently provides its number-field specialization; the extension is recorded as a gap rather than silently supplied by it.
proofSteps: Spread out over O_{k,S}; integral points have fibres of bounded degree and ramification, so finitely many fibre types and an infinite set of places splitting all of them; at one such place the Lang–Weil estimate gives a local point that does not split, an open set avoided by X(k) (Poonen Theorem 8.4.10, Corollary 8.4.11).
acceptance: 𝔾_m over ℚ with the squaring cover fails strong approximation off ∞.

sources.locator: §8.4.6, Theorem 8.4.10 and Corollary 8.4.11 with proofs, pp. 243–244
sources.match: Minchev's theorem: a nontrivial finite étale cover prevents strong approximation.

nodes.title: Insufficiency of the Brauer–Manin and descent obstructions
nodes.statement: (a) There is a nice ℚ-variety X (Skorobogatov's bielliptic surface, birational to (x² + 1)y² = (x² + 2)z² = 3(t⁴ − 54t² − 117t − 243)) with X(𝔸)^{Br} ≠ ∅ but X(ℚ) = ∅; its emptiness is explained by X(𝔸)^{ét,Br} = ∅, equivalently by a single torsor under a noncommutative finite étale group. (b) There is a nice ℚ-variety (Poonen's quadric bundle over a curve) with X(𝔸)^{ét,Br} ≠ ∅ but X(ℚ) = ∅, so even the descent obstruction is insufficient. In particular a nonempty Brauer–Manin set does not imply a rational point.
hypotheses: Explicit constructions over ℚ; the statements are existence theorems.
proofSteps: (a) Brauer–Manin applied to the étale double cover Y → X by a product of genus-one curves and its twists (Poonen §8.6.1, Theorem 8.6.1, Remark 8.6.4).
(b) Poonen §8.6.2, Theorem 8.6.5 and Propositions 8.6.6–8.6.10, combined with etale-brauer-equals-descent.
acceptance: Both examples are compatible with X(ℚ) ⊆ X(𝔸)^{ét,Br}.

sources.locator: §8.6.1–8.6.2, Theorem 8.6.1, Definition 8.6.2, Remark 8.6.4, Theorem 8.6.5, Propositions 8.6.6–8.6.10, pp. 248–252
sources.match: Skorobogatov's bielliptic counterexample beyond Brauer–Manin and Poonen's counterexample beyond étale–Brauer.

nodes.title: Curves with good reduction outside S
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field and S a finite set of places containing the archimedean ones. A smooth projective geometrically connected curve C over K has good reduction outside S if it extends to a smooth proper morphism 𝒞 → Spec O_{K,S} with geometrically connected fibres. Shafarevich's set Sh(K, S, g) is the set of K-isomorphism classes of such curves of genus g. The Shafarevich finiteness statement for (K, S, g) is the assertion that Sh(K, S, g) is finite.
hypotheses: S finite, containing the archimedean places; g ≥ 0.
proofSteps: Smooth proper models over Dedekind bases (SchemeAndStackFoundations SF.3 models of curves); the predicate is stated as the existence of such a model.
acceptance: ℙ¹_K has good reduction everywhere; an elliptic curve has good reduction outside the primes dividing its minimal discriminant.

sources.locator: §2.1, definition of Shafarevich sets and Exemple 1.1, pp. 85–86
sources.match: Shafarevich sets of isomorphism classes of families over B = Spec O − S with prescribed fibres; finiteness of extensions of bounded degree unramified outside S (Hermite).

sources.locator: Chapter IV, §1 (statement of the Shafarevich conjecture) and §5, pp. 132–133, 145
sources.match: Curves with good reduction outside a finite set of primes and Shafarevich's conjecture.

uses.how: the Kodaira–Parshin curves C_P have good reduction outside a fixed set
Faltings' Korollar 1 to Satz 6: Sh(K, S, g) is finite for g ≥ 2

nodes.title: The Chevalley–Weil theorem
nodes.statement: Let k be a number field and f : Z → X a finite étale morphism of varieties over k with X proper (or, for integral points, a finite étale morphism of separated schemes of finite type over O_{k,S}). Then there is a finite extension k'/k such that X(k) ⊆ f(Z(k')); for integral points, every x ∈ 𝒳(O_{k,S}) lifts to Z over a field of degree ≤ deg f unramified outside S ∪ (ramification of the model), and these fields form a finite set (Hermite).
hypotheses: f finite étale; X proper for the rational-point form.
proofSteps: Rational points: f is a torsor under a finite étale group after passing to a Galois closure, and Poonen Corollary 8.4.8 gives k' (RP.3/selmer-set-of-torsor).

Integral points: fibres are finite étale O_{k,S}-schemes of degree deg f, unramified outside S; finitely many such by Hermite's theorem (ArithmeticGaloisDuality R02.3/hermite-unramified-outside-finite).
acceptance: For the étale double cover of y² = (x² + 1)(x⁴ + 1) by c w² = x⁴ + 1, k' = ℚ(√2) suffices.

sources.locator: §8.4.4, Corollary 8.4.8 and proof, p. 242; §8.4.6, proof of Theorem 8.4.10, p. 243
sources.match: A finite separable extension over which all rational points lift through a torsor over a proper variety; integral points have fibres of bounded degree and ramification, so finitely many fibre types.
Finiteness of finite étale O − S-schemes of given degree (Hermite).

nodes.title: De Franchis' theorem
nodes.statement: Let C' and C be smooth projective curves over a field k of characteristic zero with genus(C) ≥ 2. Then there are only finitely many nonconstant morphisms C' → C.
hypotheses: genus(C) ≥ 2; C, C' smooth projective over k.
Characteristic zero for the assertion about all nonconstant morphisms. In positive characteristic use separable morphisms; unrestricted Frobenius iterates invalidate finiteness.
proofSteps: Milne Chapter IV Theorem 5.2 (reference to Lang): nonconstant maps C' → C have bounded degree by Riemann–Hurwitz, form a scheme of finite type (Hom scheme), and a rigidity argument shows the relevant components are points; equivalently, the induced homomorphisms Jac C' → Jac C form a discrete subset of a finitely generated group with bounded degree.
acceptance: For C' = C of genus ≥ 2, Aut(C) is finite (a special case).
Over a finite field a genus≥2 curve has infinitely many nonconstant Frobenius self-maps. The separability or characteristic-zero qualification is essential.

sources.match: For C of genus at least 2 there are only finitely many nonconstant maps C' → C.

nodes.title: The Kodaira–Parshin construction
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, S a finite set of places containing the archimedean and dyadic ones, and C/K a smooth projective curve of genus g ≥ 1 with good reduction outside S. There are a finite extension L/K and, for every P ∈ C(K), a curve C_P over L and a finite morphism φ_P : C_P → C_L such that: (i) C_P has good reduction outside the places of L above S; (ii) the genus of C_P is bounded in terms of g (Szpiro: 2g(C_P) − 2 = 2^{2g}(4g − 3) for the double cover of the 2-isogeny pullback); (iii) φ_P is ramified exactly above P. Construction: pull back multiplication by 2 on the Jacobian along the Abel–Jacobi map Q ↦ [Q − P] to get an unramified cover C₁ → C of degree 2^{2g}; the preimage D of P has degree 2^{2g}; over an extension of degree ≤ 2^{2g₁} unramified outside S, where g₁=1+2^{2g}(g−1) is the genus of C₁, O(D) ≅ M^{⊗2}, and C_P is the double cover of C₁ ramified exactly along D defined by M; L is the compositum of the finitely many fields so obtained.
hypotheses: S contains the archimedean and dyadic places; g ≥ 1 (g ≥ 2 is used only in the application through de Franchis).
proofSteps: The unramified cover C₁ → C from the 2-isogeny of the Jacobian (JacobianChallenge Layer F Abel–Jacobi; AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli A3 multiplication by 2), with good reduction outside S since [2] is étale away from dyadic places.

Halve the class of the full branch divisor D in Pic(C₁), using multiplication by two on Jac(C₁). Its fibre has degree 2^{2g₁}, so this is a safe extension-degree bound; 2^{2g} is not justified for this step. The fibre is finite étale outside S; use Hermite–Minkowski/Chevalley–Weil to choose one common finite compositum.
Double covers in residue characteristic ≠ 2 ramify exactly where the order of the defining function is odd (Milne IV §5 remarks), giving (i) and (iii); Riemann–Hurwitz gives (ii).

This is Szpiro’s full branch-divisor construction, pp.97–98. Milne IV §5 uses a two-point branch variant with a different genus. Keep the two constructions distinct; the displayed full-branch genus is g_P=1+2^{2g−1}(4g−3).
acceptance: For g = 1, taking P as origin identifies C with its Jacobian, and C₁ → C is multiplication by 2.

sources.locator: Chapter IV, §5, Theorem 5.1 and its proof, pp. 145–148
sources.match: The Kodaira–Parshin construction: a finite extension L and covers C_P → C_L with good reduction outside S, bounded genus and ramification exactly at P.
The construction via the pullback of multiplication by 2 on the Jacobian, halving the divisor D over an extension étale outside S, and the double cover ramified along D; Mumford's variant.

uses.how: Shafarevich finiteness and de Franchis make P ↦ C_P finite-to-one
Faltings' Satz 7 is the composite of this construction with Korollar 1 to Satz 6
Lawrence–Venkatesh use a Hurwitz-space variant with Aff(q)-covers branched at one point

nodes.title: Parshin: Shafarevich finiteness implies Mordell
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field and C/K a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus g ≥ 2. Let L, S' and g' be the data of kodaira-parshin-construction for C. If the Shafarevich finiteness statement holds for (L, S', g'), then C(K) is finite.
hypotheses: The Shafarevich finiteness for curves over L of the bounded genus g' with good reduction outside S' is a hypothesis (supplied unconditionally by FaltingsFinitenessAndIsogenyTheorems R28.5).
proofSteps: By hypothesis the curves C_P, P ∈ C(K), fall into finitely many isomorphism classes over L.
For a fixed curve X over L, each P with C_P ≅ X gives a nonconstant map X → C_L ramified exactly above P, and distinct P give distinct maps; de Franchis (g ≥ 2) bounds their number (Milne IV §5).
acceptance: For g = 1 the argument fails exactly at de Franchis: an elliptic curve of positive rank has infinitely many rational points.

sources.locator: Chapter IV, §5, deduction of Mordell from Theorems 5.1 and 5.2, p. 146
sources.match: Shafarevich's conjecture with the Kodaira–Parshin construction and de Franchis gives finiteness of C(K).
The map from C(K) to the Shafarevich set has finite fibres since C_P → C is ramified only at P and there are finitely many maps between curves of genus ≥ 2.

nodes.title: The Mordell conjecture (Faltings' theorem)
nodes.statement: For a smooth projective geometrically connected curve C of genus≥2 over a number field K, C(K) is finite. This roadmap owns one proposed declaration, with the independent Vojta–Bombieri route at RP.5/vojta-bombieri-mordell. The Parshin route at RP.4/parshin-implication remains a conditional comparison requiring finiteness of curves of fixed genus with good reduction outside S; that hypothesis is not imported from the higher-tier Faltings roadmap. FaltingsFinitenessAndIsogenyTheorems and MordellLawrenceVenkatesh may import the present rational-point theorem and Parshin construction when their later plans are synchronized.
hypotheses: K a number field; g ≥ 2.
proofSteps: Use RP.5/vojta-bombieri-mordell for the unconditional declaration; its prerequisite graph uses neither this node nor Shafarevich finiteness.
Record RP.4/parshin-implication as a separate conditional proof route. Do not treat a missing lower-tier supplier for Shafarevich finiteness as discharged by an upward dependency.
acceptance: For y² = (x² + 1)(x⁴ + 1) over ℚ (genus 2), the finite set has eight points (RP.3/descent-worked-example).
The theorem gives no bound on heights and no algorithm.

sources.match: Faltings' theorem; Parshin's reduction to Shafarevich's conjecture; ineffectivity of all known proofs.
Statement of Mordell's conjecture as proved by Faltings.

nodes.title: S-integral points on affine curves
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, S a finite set of places containing the archimedean ones, X an affine curve over K with smooth projective completion X̄, and 𝒳 a model of X over O_{K,S} (an affine O_{K,S}-scheme of finite type with generic fibre X). The S-integral points are 𝒳(O_{K,S}) ⊆ X(K). Different models give sets that differ by enlarging S; finiteness of 𝒳(O_{K,S}) for every model and every S is independent of the choices.
hypotheses: X affine; the model is affine of finite type over O_{K,S}.
proofSteps: Models exist by spreading out and agree over O_{K,T} for T ⊇ S large (RP.2/integral-model-exists-unique).
acceptance: For X = 𝔾_m = 𝔸¹ ∖ {0} with model Spec O_{K,S}[t, 1/t], the S-integral points are the S-units O_{K,S}^×.

sources.locator: §1, statement of Siegel's theorem and the description of integral points as sections, p. 84
sources.match: Integral points of an affine curve with respect to S as sections of a model over Spec O − S.

uses.how: finiteness of S-integral points
S-unit equations are integral points on ℙ¹ minus three points

nodes.title: Siegel's theorem on integral points
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, S a finite set of places containing the archimedean ones, and X an affine curve over K with smooth projective completion X̄ of genus g. If g ≥ 1, or g = 0 and X̄ ∖ X has at least three geometric points, then 𝒳(O_{K,S}) is finite for every model 𝒳. The theorem is ineffective in general.
hypotheses: X affine, geometrically irreducible; the boundary counted over K̄.
proofSteps: Reduction: by Chevalley–Weil, replace X by an unramified cover (pulled back from multiplication on the Jacobian when g ≥ 1) and K by a finite extension, so that the boundary has at least three points defined over K.

Corvaja–Zannier, pp.267–271: choose V_N of functions with poles bounded by N times the boundary. Riemann–Roch gives its dimension and bases with controlled vanishing at each boundary point. For each v∈S choose the relevant boundary point and its basis, then apply the number-field S-adic Subspace Theorem to these systems of independent linear forms. The pole/vanishing inequality confines integral points to finitely many proper linear sections; on a curve each section is finite. The rational-only product form is insufficient; request the precise number-field corollary of DT.2/absolute-subspace-theorem-for-systems.
Genus 0 with three boundary points is the S-unit equation (DT.2).
acceptance: The S-unit equation u + v = 1 in units of ℤ[1/2] has exactly the three solutions (2, −1), (−1, 2), (1/2, 1/2).

sources.match: Finiteness of S-integral points on an affine curve when the genus is positive or the genus is zero with at least three points at infinity; no effective bound.

sources.locator: Main theorem (C. R. Math. Acad. Sci. Paris 334 (2002), 267–271)
sources.match: A proof of Siegel's theorem by the Subspace Theorem for curves with at least three points at infinity.

nodes.title: The Mordell conjecture over function fields
nodes.statement: Let K be a function field with field of constants k (K = k(V), k algebraically closed in K) and X a regular projective geometrically integral K-curve of genus > 1 with X(K) infinite. If char k = 0, X is constant (X ≅ Y_K for a k-curve Y); if char k = p > 0, X is isotrivial (constant after a finite extension of K). Constant curves over ℂ(t) and Frobenius twists over 𝔽_q(t) show that the hypotheses cannot be dropped.
hypotheses: K a function field with constant field k; X of genus > 1.
proofSteps: Manin, Grauert (characteristic 0) and Samuel, Voloch (characteristic p), as recorded in Poonen Theorem 9.5.10; induction on the transcendence degree reduces to trdeg K/k = 1.
acceptance: For K = ℂ(t) and X = (X₀)_K, X(K) ⊇ X₀(ℂ) is infinite.

sources.match: Over function fields, curves of genus > 1 with infinitely many points are constant (characteristic 0) or isotrivial (characteristic p).

nodes.title: Abelian subvarieties, cosets and quotients
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety over a field k. An abelian subvariety is a closed subgroup scheme B ⊆ A that is an abelian variety (smooth, connected, proper). A coset is a translate x + B with B an abelian subvariety and x ∈ A(k̄); a torsion coset is one with x torsion; a torsion subvariety is a finite union of torsion cosets. For every abelian subvariety B the quotient A → A/B exists as an abelian variety with kernel B, and by Poincaré reducibility there is a complementary abelian subvariety B' with B + B' = A and B ∩ B' finite.
hypotheses: k any field; cosets are taken over k̄ unless stated.
proofSteps: Quotients by abelian subvarieties: the fppf quotient sheaf A/B (SF.1/quotient-sheaf) is an algebraic space by Artin's theorem (SF.1/artin-bootstrap), a proper smooth connected group space over a field, hence an abelian variety; over a field this is Conrad Theorem 3.7 for quotients by closed subgroups (Xie–Yuan, proof of Proposition 3.6). AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli A3 treats finite subgroups only.
Complements: Poincaré complete reducibility (AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli A6/poincare-complete-reducibility).
acceptance: In A = E × E, the diagonal and the antidiagonal are abelian subvarieties meeting in E[2].

sources.locator: proof of Proposition 3.6, p. 16; proof of Lemma 5.3, p. 24
sources.match: Quotients A → A/B by abelian subvarieties and the image X/Stab⁰(X).
Quotients of finite type group schemes over a field by closed subgroups.

nodes.title: Stabilizers of subvarieties
nodes.statement: For a closed subvariety X of an abelian variety A over k, Stab(X) is the closed subgroup scheme of a ∈ A with a + X = X, and Stab⁰(X) its identity component (reduced), an abelian subvariety. X is a union of cosets of Stab⁰(X) and X/Stab⁰(X) ⊆ A/Stab⁰(X) has finite stabilizer. If X is irreducible and embedded in projective space by a very ample L, deg_L Stab(X) ≤ (deg_L X)^{dim X + 1}.
hypotheses: X closed in A; for the degree bound X irreducible and L very ample.

Use an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero for the scheme stabilizer and its degree bound here. For perfect fields the reduced identity component is smooth; a nonreduced stabilizer in characteristic p cannot be silently replaced in scheme-fibre assertions.
proofSteps: Stab(X) is the intersection over x ∈ X(k̄) of X − x, a closed subgroup (representability of the transporter).
The degree bound: David–Hindry Lemme 2.1(ii) via intersection of finitely many translates (as cited by Gao–Habegger).
acceptance: Stab(A) = A; Stab({x}) = {0}; for X = x + B, Stab⁰(X) = B.

sources.locator: proof of Proposition 6.9, p. 38; proof of Proposition 8.1, p. 47

nodes.title: The abelian subvariety generated by X − X
nodes.statement: For an irreducible closed subvariety X of an abelian variety A over an algebraically closed field, the abelian subvariety A' generated by X − X is the g-fold sum (X − X) + ⋯ + (X − X) (g = dim A); X ⊆ A' + Q for some Q ∈ A(k), and X generates A when A' = A. Translation preserves the property. With L very ample, deg_L(Y + Y') ≤ 4^{dim Y + dim Y'}·deg_L Y·deg_L Y' for irreducible Y, Y' ⊆ A, and deg_L A' ≪_g (deg_L X)^{2g}.
hypotheses: k algebraically closed; X irreducible; L very ample (replace L by L^{⊗3} in the degree argument).
proofSteps: Sums of irreducible subvarieties stabilise after g steps by dimension count; the stable sum is a subgroup, hence an abelian subvariety.
Degree of sums: Gao–Ge–Kühne Lemma 2.4 (projection from the addition map on A × A).
Degree of A′: iterate Lemma 2.4 along the g-fold sum (Gao–Ge–Kühne Lemma 2.5, argument of Hindry), retaining the per-step factor 4^{dim Y+dim Y′} from Lemma 2.4.
acceptance: For a curve C of genus ≥ 1 embedded in its Jacobian J, C − C generates J (AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli A6/curve-generated-subvariety).

sources.match: X generates A; A′ is the g-fold sum of X−X; Lemmas 2.4–2.5 give the degree bounds for sums and A′ in the arXiv v4 read.

nodes.title: The Ueno locus
nodes.statement: For a closed subvariety X of an abelian variety A over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, the Ueno locus Z(X) is the union of all positive-dimensional cosets contained in X, and X° = X ∖ Z(X). Z(X) is Zariski closed (Kawamata), so X° is open. (X − P)° = X° − P, and (X')° ⊇ X° ∩ X' for closed X' ⊆ X. The positive-dimensional abelian subvarieties B maximal with x + B ⊆ X for some x form a finite set Σ(X; A) with deg_L B and #Σ(X; A) bounded in terms of dim A and deg_L X (Bogomolov; Rémond), and Z(X) = ⋃_{B ∈ Σ(X;A)} (X_B + B) with X_B = ⋂_{b ∈ B} (X − b) ∩ B^⊥ a finite intersection of at most dim X translates.
hypotheses: k algebraically closed of characteristic 0; X closed in A.

For the quoted uniform degree bound on B^⊥ and X_B, assume X generates A, or replace A by the abelian subvariety generated by X−X. An arbitrary fixed Poincaré complement has no asserted uniform degree bound.
proofSteps: Closedness: Kawamata's structure theorem for subvarieties with positive-dimensional stabilizer (Ueno fibration), as cited by Gao–Ge–Kühne.
Finiteness and degree bounds of maximal cosets: Bogomolov 1981 Theorem 1 and Rémond Proposition 4.1, Lemma 4.6, as cited by Gao–Ge–Kühne and Gao–Habegger.

GGK Lemma 7.4, pp.43–44, uses the generating hypothesis when choosing B^⊥ with controlled degree. Positive dimension of B allows dimension descent to a finite intersection of at most dim X translates; this count is not itself an error.
acceptance: For a curve of genus ≥ 2 in its Jacobian, the Ueno locus is empty.

nodes.title: Subgroups of finite rank
nodes.statement: A subgroup Γ of an abelian group G (for example A(F) for an abelian variety A over a field F) has finite rank if Γ ⊗_ℤ ℚ is a finite-dimensional ℚ-vector space; rk Γ = dim_ℚ(Γ ⊗ ℚ). Equivalently Γ is contained in the division hull {x : Nx ∈ Γ₀ for some N ≥ 1} of a finitely generated subgroup Γ₀ of the same rank. No End(A)-stability is required.
hypotheses: G abelian.
The torsion subgroup is not finitely generated only for an abelian variety of positive dimension in the stated algebraically closed characteristic-zero test.
proofSteps: Choose Γ₀ generated by lifts of a ℚ-basis of Γ ⊗ ℚ; every x ∈ Γ has a multiple in Γ₀.
acceptance: A(K) has finite rank by Mordell–Weil. If dim A>0 over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, A(K̄)_tors has rank zero and is not finitely generated; dimension zero is excluded from the latter claim.

nodes.title: The Manin–Mumford theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 and X ⊆ A a closed subvariety. Then the Zariski closure of X ∩ A_tors is a torsion subvariety (a finite union of torsion cosets contained in X). Equivalently, if X ∩ A_tors is Zariski dense in X then X is a torsion subvariety. Positive-dimensional torsion cosets are legitimate infinite components.
hypotheses: Characteristic 0 (in positive characteristic see manin-mumford-positive-characteristic).
proofSteps: Raynaud 1983 (curves and subvarieties; p-adic methods); over number fields Hindry 1988 Theorem 1 via lower bounds for Galois orbits of torsion points; the specialisation argument reduces ℂ to ℚ̄.
It is the case Γ = A_tors (rank 0) of mordell-lang, but its proofs are independent.
acceptance: For a curve C of genus ≥ 2 in its Jacobian by an Abel–Jacobi embedding, C ∩ J_tors is finite.

sources.locator: Theorem 3.2 and proof, p. 13, citing Raynaud 1983, Hindry 1988 Theorem 1, Hrushovski 2001, Scanlon 2004
sources.match: Manin–Mumford in characteristic 0 in a uniform form.
The Manin–Mumford statement (Raynaud over number fields).

nodes.title: Manin–Mumford for trivial trace in positive characteristic
nodes.statement: In characteristic p>0, let K be finitely generated over an algebraically closed field k and A an abelian variety over K with trivial geometric K̄/k-trace. If X ⊆ A_{K̄} is a closed subvariety with X(K̄) ∩ A(K̄)_tors Zariski dense in X, then X is a torsion subvariety. The proof covers all torsion, including p-power torsion.
hypotheses: Characteristic p>0; trivial geometric K̄/k-trace; k algebraically closed.
The trace is the geometric trace of A_{K̄} over the algebraically closed constant field k, as specified by Xie–Yuan §1.1; zero original K/k-trace is not enough.
proofSteps: Scanlon's positive-characteristic Manin–Mumford theorem (Theorem 2.2): the closure of X ∩ G_tors is a finite union of special subvarieties a + h^{-1}(X₀) with h : G → G₀ and X₀ defined over 𝔽̄_p (Pink–Roessler 2004 for the full torsion).

Trivial geometric trace excludes nonzero homomorphisms to abelian varieties over 𝔽̄_p ⊆ k (kk-trace universal property), so special subvarieties are torsion cosets (Xie–Yuan, review note on Theorem 5.1).
acceptance: For A with trivial trace and X a curve of genus ≥ 2, X ∩ A_tors is finite.

A nonconstant quadratic isotrivial twist of a constant Jacobian in characteristic p≠2 can have zero K/k-trace while becoming constant over K(√t). Over K̄ its constant genus≥2 curve has dense torsion over F̄_p and is not a torsion coset. This rules out the original-trace-only hypothesis.

sources.match: Manin–Mumford for trivial trace over finitely generated fields in arbitrary characteristic (Hrushovski; Pink–Roessler).
Positive-characteristic Manin–Mumford for all torsion, with special subvarieties defined over finite fields.

nodes.title: Uniform Manin–Mumford in families
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety over an algebraically closed field K of characteristic 0, V an irreducible quasi-projective K-variety and Y ⊆ V × A an irreducible closed subvariety with fibres Y_v. There are a finite set 𝓜 of abelian subvarieties of A and an integer D such that for every v ∈ V(K) the Zariski closure of Y_v ∩ A_tors is a union of at most D translates of members of 𝓜 by torsion points.
hypotheses: Characteristic 0; Y irreducible closed in V × A.
proofSteps: Scanlon's automatic uniformity (2004 Theorem 2.4) via the model theory of algebraically closed fields with a generic automorphism (Hrushovski), as cited by Gao–Habegger Theorem 3.2 (statement misprint E1 corrected).
acceptance: For V a point this is manin-mumford.

sources.match: Uniform Manin–Mumford in algebraic families in characteristic 0, citing Raynaud, Scanlon, Hrushovski, Hindry.

nodes.title: Faltings' theorem on rational points of subvarieties of abelian varieties
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety over a number field K and X ⊆ A a closed subvariety. Then X(K) is contained in a finite union of cosets x_i + B_i contained in X; consequently X(K) ∩ X° is finite, where X° is the complement of the Ueno locus. In particular, if X contains no positive-dimensional coset (for example a curve of genus ≥ 2 in its Jacobian), X(K) is finite.
hypotheses: K a number field; X closed in A.
proofSteps: Faltings 1991 (Diophantine approximation on abelian varieties): Vojta's method generalised to subvarieties, with Faltings' product theorem and an arithmetic Riemann–Roch input; induction on dim X through the Ueno fibration (as cited by Gao–Ge–Kühne §1).
For curves the elementary version is Bombieri's (vojta-inequality and mumford-gap).

Finiteness of X°∩Γ is a consequence of the full coset decomposition, not a standalone equivalent assertion: it contains no information about Γ-points inside the Ueno locus without an additional induction.
acceptance: For C ⊆ J a curve of genus ≥ 2, this reproves Faltings' theorem on curves (RP.4/mordell-faltings).

sources.locator: §1, Theorem 1.1 and its finite-rank Mordell–Lang context, arXiv:2105.15085v4 pp.2–3
sources.match: Faltings' theorem as the finitely generated case of Mordell–Lang; X(K) ∩ X° finite.

sources.locator: §9.5.3, statement of Faltings' theorem on subvarieties of abelian varieties after Conjecture 9.5.11
sources.match: Rational points on subvarieties of abelian varieties lie in finitely many cosets.

nodes.title: Vojta's inequality
nodes.statement: Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus g≥2 over a number field k, embedded in J using a degree-one divisor class after a finite extension if needed, with the theta Néron–Tate norm. Bombieri §10 Thm.1 gives an effectively determined γ(C)>1 such that if z,w∈C(k), ‖z‖≥γ(C) and ‖w‖≥γ(C)‖z‖, then ⟨z,w⟩≤(3/4)‖z‖‖w‖. Use the same normalization for the threshold and norm ratio; an arbitrary rescaling changes the threshold. The proof needs the product/Roth lemma in §§6–9, recorded separately as unresolved proof input.
hypotheses: C of genus ≥ 2; k a number field; heights normalised as Néron–Tate heights for the theta divisor.
proofSteps: Construct the Vojta divisor on C × C and a small section by Siegel's lemma (Bombieri §§3, 8); lower bound for its height at (z, w) (§6); upper bound by Mumford's method (§5); derivative estimates and Roth's lemma bound the index (§§7, 9); combine in §10.
acceptance: The inequality excludes infinitely many points in a narrow cone; combined with mumford-gap it gives finiteness.

sources.match: The Vojta divisor, Siegel's lemma, Mumford's method, Roth's lemma, and Theorem 1: an effective angle inequality for pairs of rational points of large and very different heights.

nodes.title: Mumford's gap principle
nodes.statement: Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus g ≥ 2 over a number field k embedded in its Jacobian. There are constants c(C) and an angle θ₀ > 0 such that for distinct z, w ∈ C(k) with |z| ≥ c(C), |w| ≥ |z| and angle between z and w (for the Néron–Tate inner product) at most θ₀, one has |w| ≥ 2|z|. Consequently the points of C(k) in any cone of small angle have Néron–Tate norms growing geometrically, and the number of rational points of norm ≤ T is O(log T).
hypotheses: g ≥ 2; heights as in vojta-inequality.
proofSteps: Mumford's formula: the height on C × C of the diagonal is, up to bounded functions, a quadratic expression in Néron–Tate heights that is indefinite for g ≥ 2 and bounded below off the diagonal (Bombieri §4–§5, Lemmas 1–2).

Bombieri §10 p.639: (‖z‖²+‖w‖²)/(2g)−⟨z,w⟩ ≥ −c(1+‖z‖+‖w‖), for distinct curve points. For sufficiently large norms in a cone whose pairwise cosine exceeds 3/4, assuming 1≤‖w‖/‖z‖<2 makes the leading term negative, a contradiction; hence the ratio is at least two. Northcott handles the bounded initial region.
acceptance: With vojta-inequality: points in a cone either have bounded norm or violate Vojta, so C(k) ∩ cone is finite; finitely many cones cover the finite-dimensional J(k) ⊗ ℝ.

sources.match: Mumford's method: the height of the diagonal on C × C in terms of Néron–Tate heights; gap principle for rational points.

nodes.title: Faltings' theorem by the Vojta–Bombieri route
nodes.statement: Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus g ≥ 2 over a number field k. Then C(k) is finite. This is the same declaration as RP.4/mordell-faltings, proved here without Shafarevich finiteness: J(k) ⊗ ℝ is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space (Mordell–Weil and positive definiteness), and vojta-inequality and mumford-gap leave only finitely many points in each of finitely many cones.
hypotheses: k a number field; g ≥ 2.
proofSteps: Embed C in J; J(k) is finitely generated (RP.1/mordell-weil) and ĥ is positive definite on J(k) ⊗ ℝ (RP.1/neron-tate-positive-definite).

Cover J(k) ⊗ ℝ by finitely many cones of angle < cos⁻¹(3/4); in each, mumford-gap forces geometric growth and vojta-inequality bounds the ratio, leaving finitely many points (Bombieri §10, Theorem 2).

Bombieri Thm.2 bounds the number of points above a specified norm threshold in terms of rank and γ. Northcott gives finiteness below that threshold but does not make the theorem an effective enumeration or a bound on every rational-point height.
acceptance: Bombieri's Theorem 2 gives an explicit bound for the number of rational points, not for their heights.

sources.match: Proof of the Mordell conjecture by Vojta's inequality and Mumford's gap principle, with an effective bound on the number of points.
Vojta's proof and Bombieri's elementary version of Faltings' theorem.

nodes.title: The Mordell–Lang theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety over an algebraically closed field F of characteristic 0, X ⊆ A a closed subvariety and Γ ⊆ A(F) a subgroup of finite rank. Then X(F) ∩ Γ is a finite union of sets (x_i + B_i(F)) ∩ Γ with x_i + B_i ⊆ X cosets; consequently X° ∩ Γ is finite. Special cases: Γ = A(K) finitely generated (faltings-subvarieties), Γ = A_tors (manin-mumford).
hypotheses: Characteristic 0; Γ of finite rank (finite-rank-subgroup).
proofSteps: Finitely generated Γ over a number field: faltings-subvarieties. Specialisation reduces finitely generated F to number fields (Raynaud, Hindry).
Finite rank: Γ lies in the division hull of a finitely generated Γ₀; McQuillan 1995 combined with Hindry's Galois-orbit argument handles division points (as cited by Gao–Ge–Kühne §1).

Finiteness of X°∩Γ is a consequence of the full coset decomposition, not a standalone equivalent assertion: it contains no information about Γ-points inside the Ueno locus without an additional induction.
acceptance: For X a curve of genus ≥ 2 in its Jacobian and Γ the division hull of J(K), X ∩ Γ is finite.

sources.locator: §1, Theorem 1.1 and its finite-rank Mordell–Lang context, arXiv:2105.15085v4 pp.2–3

nodes.title: The Faltings–Zhang difference map
nodes.statement: For an abelian variety A and M ≥ 1, D_M : A^{M+1} → A^M, (P₀, …, P_M) ↦ (P₁ − P₀, …, P_M − P₀). For a subvariety X ⊆ A, D_M restricts to X^{M+1} → A^M. In families of curves over S → M_g it is built from Pic¹ × Pic¹ → Jac by differences, landing in 𝔄_g^{[M]} ×_{A_g} S.
hypotheses: M ≥ 1 (the source states M ≥ 2 on p. 6 but uses D₁).
proofSteps: A morphism of abelian varieties composed with translations; its restriction to X^{M+1} is proper.
acceptance: D₁ on X × X is the difference map (x, y) ↦ y − x.

nodes.title: Zhang's difference-map lemma
nodes.statement: For an irreducible closed subvariety X of an abelian variety A with finite stabilizer there is M₀ such that for M ≥ M₀ the generic fibre of D_M : X^{M+1} → A^M is a single orbit of Stab(X) acting diagonally; in particular D_M|_{X^{M+1}} is generically finite onto its image.
hypotheses: X irreducible with finite stabilizer.
The scheme-fibre/orbit statement is in characteristic zero. A geometric-point stabilizer identity alone cannot prove equality with a nonreduced scheme stabilizer in characteristic p.
proofSteps: Fibres of D_M over a point are intersections of translates of X; for M large these stabilise to Stab(X) (Zhang 1998, proof of Lemma 3.1, as recalled by Gao–Ge–Kühne).
acceptance: For a curve of genus ≥ 2 in its Jacobian, D₂ is generically finite on C³.

sources.match: For finite stabilizer and M large the generic fibre of D₀ : X^{M+1} → A^M is a Stab(X)-orbit.

nodes.title: The minimal torsion subvariety containing X
nodes.statement: For an irreducible closed subvariety X of an abelian variety A over an algebraically closed field, T_X is the smallest torsion coset of A containing X; for a ∈ T_X torsion, T_X − a is an abelian subvariety. X is a torsion coset iff X = T_X.
hypotheses: X irreducible.
proofSteps: Intersections of torsion cosets containing X are finite unions of torsion cosets; irreducibility selects one component; descending chain condition on abelian subvarieties.
acceptance: For a torsion point t, T_{{t}} = {t}; for a non-torsion point x of an elliptic curve E, T_{{x}} = E.

nodes.title: The essential minimum of a subvariety
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety over a number field (or a polarized function field) K, L a symmetric ample line bundle and X ⊆ A_{K̄} a nonempty irreducible closed subvariety. The essential minimum is μ_ess(X) = sup over proper closed Y ⊊ X of inf{ĥ_L(x) : x ∈ X(K̄) ∖ Y(K̄)}; equivalently the infimum of the ε ≥ 0 such that {x ∈ X(K̄) : ĥ_L(x) ≤ ε} is Zariski dense in X. X has dense small points iff μ_ess(X) = 0.
hypotheses: L symmetric ample; ĥ_L the Néron–Tate height.

X is nonempty and irreducible. The zero-height/torsion tests and μ_ess=0 iff torsion-coset theorem use number fields; geometric function-field constants require the trace correction and are not covered by that equivalence.
proofSteps: Monotone in Y; independent of the field of definition by the Galois invariance of ĥ.
acceptance: For X a torsion coset, μ_ess(X) = 0.

sources.match: Bogomolov's conjecture for curves stated as a positive lower bound for heights outside a finite set.

uses.how: Over number fields, Bogomolov says μ_ess(X)>0 unless X is a torsion coset; function-field constant/trace subvarieties require the corresponding geometric correction.

nodes.title: The Bogomolov conjecture (Ullmo–Zhang)
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety over a number field K, L a symmetric ample line bundle and X ⊆ A_{K̄} an irreducible closed subvariety that is not a torsion coset. Then μ_ess(X) > 0: there is ε > 0 such that {x ∈ X(K̄) : ĥ_L(x) < ε} is not Zariski dense in X. For a curve of genus ≥ 2 embedded in its Jacobian, the set of points of height < ε is finite (Ullmo). Manin–Mumford alone (height zero) does not imply this.
hypotheses: K a number field (characteristic 0); X not a torsion coset.
proofSteps: Reduce to X with finite stabilizer that generates A (quotient by Stab⁰(X), minimal-torsion-subvariety).

Suppose small points are dense; by Szpiro–Ullmo–Zhang equidistribution (szpiro-ullmo-zhang-equidistribution) generic small sequences on X^{M+1} and on D_M(X^{M+1}) equidistribute to the canonical measures.

Zhang's difference lemma makes D_M generically finite; comparing the pushforward of the measure on X^{M+1} with the measure on the image yields a contradiction on the support (Zhang 1998; Ullmo 1998 for curves).
acceptance: For X=x+B, assume the image of x in A/B has infinite order; x itself having infinite order does not suffice when x∈B. Then μ_ess(X)>0. An exact equality with a quotient-point height requires the specified quotient-induced orthogonal polarization; arbitrary polarizations only give the appropriate comparison/positivity.

sources.match: Bogomolov's conjecture for curves in their Jacobians, via Zhang's admissible pairing and equidistribution.

nodes.title: Equidistribution of small points on abelian varieties
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety over a number field K, L symmetric ample, X ⊆ A geometrically irreducible and defined over K (after a finite extension if needed) with μ_ess(X) = 0, and (x_n) a generic sequence in X(K̄) (no infinite subsequence lies in a proper closed subvariety of X) with ĥ_L(x_n) → 0. Then for every archimedean place v the probability measures equidistributed on the Galois orbits of x_n in X(ℂ_v) converge weakly to the normalised canonical measure c₁(L, ‖·‖_can)^{dim X}/deg_L X.
hypotheses: K a number field; (x_n) generic and small.

For the general-subvariety version use Ullmo Thm.2.4: a semipositive adelic metric with strictly positive archimedean curvature and the prescribed uniform approximation by arithmetic model metrics, with the normalized subvariety height and generic small sequence. The abelian canonical version is Thm.2.3; the general version is not inferred solely from μ_ess=0 without the metric/intersection input.

Take Galois orbits over a field of definition of X; otherwise their support can leave X and the asserted measure on X(ℂ_v) is ill-typed. Generic means that every proper closed subset contains only finitely many terms, not that no finite subsequence lies in it.
proofSteps: Szpiro–Ullmo–Zhang 1997: Zhang's successive minima inequality for adelic metrized line bundles and the variational principle with perturbed metrics.

Its inputs, the arithmetic intersection theory of adelic metrized line bundles on varieties of arbitrary dimension (arithmetic Hilbert–Samuel and successive minima), are planned by no roadmap (recorded gap).
acceptance: For an elliptic curve E over a number field, a generic sequence of torsion points has Galois-orbit measures converging to Haar measure. A constant torsion sequence is not generic and does not equidistribute.

sources.locator: §1, discussion of Zhang's admissible pairing and equidistribution, pp. 1–3

nodes.title: Hypersurface sections of abelian varieties containing no cosets
nodes.statement: Let A ⊆ ℙ^M be an abelian variety of dimension g ≥ 1 and d ≥ g − 1. There is a dense Zariski open U in the space of degree-d forms, with complement of codimension ≥ d + 2 − g, such that A ∩ 𝒵(f) contains no positive-dimensional coset for f ∈ U. For an abelian subvariety B with dim B ≥ 1 and d ≥ max{1, g − dim B}, the forms f with A ∩ 𝒵(f) containing a translate of B lie in a closed subset of codimension ≥ d + 1 + dim B − g. The Hilbert function satisfies H_V(d) ≥ binom(dim V + d, dim V) ≥ d + 1 for V ⊆ ℙ^M with dim V ≥ 1.
hypotheses: A ⊆ ℙ^M projective; d as stated.
A and the form space are over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. The good open excludes forms vanishing identically on A, including the zero form.
proofSteps: Incidence variety of (coset translate, form) and fibre dimension counts using the Hilbert function lower bound (Gao–Habegger Lemma C.2 and (C.1)).
Bogomolov's finiteness of maximal cosets reduces to finitely many B (ueno-locus); apply Lemma C.2 to each (Proposition C.1).
acceptance: For g=1, every form not identically zero on A gives a finite section; forms identically zero on A give the whole elliptic curve and lie outside U. In particular U is not the entire vector space of forms.

sources.locator: (C.1), Lemma C.2 and Proposition C.1 with corollary and proofs, pp. 59–61 (misprint E17)
sources.match: Generic hypersurface sections of abelian varieties contain no positive-dimensional coset, with codimension estimates.

nodes.title: Local solubility and the local-global principle
nodes.statement: A variety X over a number field K is locally soluble (everywhere locally soluble) if X(K_v) ≠ ∅ for every place v. X satisfies the local-global principle (Hasse principle) if X(𝔸_K) ≠ ∅ implies X(K) ≠ ∅, and weak approximation if X(K) is dense in Π_v X(K_v). For X proper, X(𝔸_K) ≠ ∅ iff X is locally soluble; for X of finite type, local solubility at the finitely many places outside a model's good set and integral points elsewhere characterise X(𝔸_K) ≠ ∅.
hypotheses: K a number field; X separated of finite type.
proofSteps: For proper X, X(𝔸_K) = Π_v X(K_v) (RP.2/adelic-points-general).
In general use RP.2/adelic-points-nonempty-iff (integral points almost everywhere, from Lang–Weil and Hensel for smooth geometrically integral fibres).
acceptance: x² + y² = 3z² is not locally soluble at 3.

sources.locator: §8.4.7 (definition of the local-global principle), p. 245; §2.6.3, pp. 49–50
sources.match: The local-global principle as the implication X(𝔸) ≠ ∅ ⇒ X(k) ≠ ∅; adelic points of proper varieties are products of local points.

nodes.title: Rational points of curves through the Abel–Jacobi embedding
nodes.statement: Let C be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus g ≥ 1 over a field K with a divisor class D₀ of degree 1 defined over K (for instance a rational point). The Abel–Jacobi map ι_{D₀} : C → J = Jac C, P ↦ [P − D₀], is a closed immersion, and C(K) = ι^{-1}(J(K)) ∩ C(K) maps bijectively onto ι(C)(K) ⊆ J(K). Hence any finiteness or structure theorem for ι(C) ∩ Γ with Γ ⊆ J(K̄) (Mordell–Lang, Manin–Mumford, Bogomolov) transfers to points of C; for g = 1, ι is an isomorphism C ≅ J and C(K) is a J(K)-torsor.
hypotheses: g ≥ 1; D₀ of degree 1 over K (for g ≥ 2 a rational point suffices; without one, use C ⊆ Pic¹ and a torsor).
proofSteps: Import the Abel–Jacobi morphism from JacobianChallenge Layer F. For genus≥1, Riemann–Roch separates geometric points under the degree-one Abel map; its differential is injective by evaluation of holomorphic differentials (canonical system has no base point). Properness plus the resulting geometric immersion gives a closed immersion. The chosen degree-one Picard point translates Pic¹ to J, even if it has no representative line bundle over K.
Points over K correspond since ι is a K-morphism and a closed immersion.
acceptance: For an elliptic curve with D₀ = O, ι is the identity; for C of genus 2 the image is a theta divisor.

sources.locator: §5.7 (Jacobians as Albanese varieties) and Example 5.12.11, pp. 138–153

nodes.title: Rational points on genus-zero curves
nodes.statement: Let C be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus 0 over a number field K. Then C is isomorphic to a smooth plane conic; C satisfies the Hasse principle; if C(K) ≠ ∅ then C ≅ ℙ¹_K, C(K) is infinite and Zariski dense, and C satisfies weak approximation. Whether C(K) ≠ ∅ is decided by finitely many local conditions (the places where the associated quaternion algebra ramifies).
hypotheses: K a number field; genus 0.
proofSteps: Anticanonical embedding as a conic (SchemeAndStackFoundations SF.3/projective-line-characterization); Hasse–Minkowski for ternary forms (GlobalQuadraticForms Layer 5); a point gives ℙ¹ by projection.
Brauer–Manin is vacuous on conics (RP.2/conic-example).
acceptance: x² + y² = z² ≅ ℙ¹_ℚ; x² + y² = 3z² has no rational point.

sources.match: One-dimensional Severi–Brauer varieties are conics and satisfy the local-global principle over global fields.

nodes.title: Rational points on genus-one curves
nodes.statement: Let C be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus 1 over a number field K with Jacobian E. Then: C is an E-torsor with class [C] ∈ H¹(K, E) (RP.3/genus-one-torsors); C(K) ≠ ∅ iff [C] = 0, and then C ≅ E and C(K) ≅ E(K) is a finitely generated group (Mordell–Weil), finite or infinite according to the rank; if C is locally soluble, [C] ∈ Ш(E/K), and C(K) = ∅ is possible (a positive proportion of locally soluble genus-one curves y² = f(x), Bhargava–Gross–Wang Theorem 10 with g = 1). If Ш(E/K) is finite, the only obstruction to C(K) ≠ ∅ is the Brauer–Manin obstruction (Manin); the finiteness of Ш remains conjectural; the preceding Brauer–Manin sufficiency statement is a proved conditional theorem and uses finiteness explicitly.
hypotheses: K a number field; genus 1.
proofSteps: Torsor classification (RP.3/genus-one-torsors); Mordell–Weil for E (TauCetiRoadmap EllipticCurves Layer 6; RP.1/mordell-weil).
Locally soluble failures: RP.3/bgw-hasse-failures.

Manin's theorem: the Cassels–Tate pairing on Ш(E/K) is computed by the Brauer–Manin pairing of algebraic classes on C (Skorobogatov, Torsors and rational points §6.2); stated conditionally on finiteness of Ш.
acceptance: The curves 2w² = x⁴ + 1 and w² = x⁴ + 1 have rational points and are elliptic curves of rank 0 (Poonen §8.3).

sources.match: Genus-one curves are torsors under their Jacobians; worked rank-zero examples.
A positive proportion of locally soluble genus-one (g = 1) curves y² = f(x) have no rational point, by a Brauer–Manin obstruction.

nodes.title: Rational points on curves of genus at least two
nodes.statement: Let C be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus g ≥ 2 over a number field K. Then C(K) is finite (Faltings), by either proof route (RP.4/mordell-faltings or RP.5/vojta-bombieri-mordell); ι(C)(K̄) ∩ Γ is finite for every finite-rank Γ ⊆ J(K̄) (Mordell–Lang); points of small Néron–Tate height on ι(C) are finite (Bogomolov). No proved theorem gives an algorithm listing C(K) in general; for curves over function fields the analogue holds for non-isotrivial curves.
hypotheses: K a number field; g ≥ 2.
Choose a degree-one Picard class after a finite extension to define ι if needed, or work in the Pic¹ torsor. The curve’s rational points transfer back by the closed immersion.
proofSteps: Faltings: RP.4/mordell-faltings; Mordell–Lang and Bogomolov on ι(C): RP.5/mordell-lang, RP.5/bogomolov, transferred by curve-in-jacobian; function fields: RP.4/function-field-mordell.
acceptance: y² = (x² + 1)(x⁴ + 1) over ℚ has exactly eight rational points (RP.3/descent-worked-example).

nodes.title: Statements of the open conjectures (no consumer treats them as proved)
nodes.statement: The following are defined as propositions, never assumed by a theorem of this roadmap: (a) Bombieri–Lang: for a geometrically integral variety X of general type over a number field K with dim X > 0, X(K) is not Zariski dense; (b) Vojta's main conjecture for a smooth projective X with canonical divisor K_X, ample A, normal crossings divisor D, finite set of places S and ε > 0: Σ_{v∈S} λ_{D,v}(x) + h_{K_X}(x) ≤ ε·h_A(x) + O(1) outside a proper Zariski closed subset; (c) Colliot-Thélène's conjecture: for smooth proper geometrically rationally connected X over a number field, X(K) is dense in X(𝔸_K)^{Br}; (d) finiteness of Ш(A/K) for abelian varieties over number fields. Each is a definition of a Prop with a precise statement; the register records which special cases are theorems (curves for (a) by Faltings; conics and Châtelet surfaces with few degenerate fibres for (c)). In (b), quantify over rational points x∈X(K) outside Supp(D)∪Z, require S to contain all archimedean places, choose Z depending on the geometric data and ε, and allow a uniform additive constant depending on the fixed data and S. This is the rational-point, untruncated ε-height form; no bounded-degree discriminant or truncated-counting version is asserted.
hypotheses: Statements only; hypotheses as in Poonen §9.5.3 and §9.2.
proofSteps: Write each statement over the carriers of this roadmap (rational points, Weil heights and local Weil functions, Brauer–Manin sets, Ш).
acceptance: For curves, (a) is Faltings' theorem (higher-genus-classification).

gaps.title: Arithmetic intersection theory of adelic metrized line bundles
gaps.detail: The Szpiro–Ullmo–Zhang equidistribution theorem needs Zhang's adelic metrized line bundles on varieties of arbitrary dimension over number fields, arithmetic intersection numbers, the arithmetic Hilbert–Samuel formula and Zhang's successive minima theorem. ArithmeticDynamics DY.4 plans equidistribution on ℙ¹ only and ArakelovGeometryAndAbelianHeights plans the Faltings height (R35.1–R35.6), so no roadmap plans this theory. Proposed owner: a Part II of ArakelovGeometryAndAbelianHeights (see restructure).

gaps.title: Faltings' proof of the subvariety theorem in higher dimension
gaps.detail: For curves the Vojta–Bombieri route is planned (vojta-inequality, mumford-gap). For subvarieties of dimension > 1, Faltings 1991 (Annals 133, not freely available) uses Faltings' product theorem and arithmetic Riemann–Roch; neither is planned in the atlas. McQuillan's theorem on division points (finite-rank case) is likewise cited, not decomposed.

gaps.title: Proofs of Manin–Mumford
gaps.detail: Raynaud 1983 (p-adic method) and Hindry 1988 (lower bounds for Galois orbits of torsion points through Serre's and Bogomolov's results on the image of Galois) are cited key theorems; their inputs are not planned. Scanlon's Theorem 2.2 is read for the positive-characteristic case.

gaps.title: Structure of the Ueno locus
gaps.detail: Kawamata's closedness theorem (Ueno fibration) and Bogomolov's 1981 finiteness of maximal cosets with Rémond's degree bounds are cited through Gao–Ge–Kühne and Gao–Habegger; the original sources were not read.

gaps.title: Manin's interpretation of Ш through the Brauer–Manin pairing
gaps.detail: The identification of the Cassels–Tate pairing with the algebraic Brauer–Manin pairing on torsors under abelian varieties (Manin 1971; Skorobogatov, Torsors and rational points §6.2, not freely available) is used as a cited key theorem; the Cassels–Tate pairing itself is not planned by this roadmap.

gaps.title: Compactness of the integers of a nonarchimedean completion of a number field
gaps.detail: O_v = v.adicCompletionIntegers K is compact for a number field K (complete, with finite residue field), which gives local compactness of the finite adeles through RestrictedProduct.locallyCompactSpace_of_group and of X(𝔸_K) through RP.2/points-topology-presentation. No compactness instance for adicCompletionIntegers is in the pinned declaration index; only the local-compactness API items use it.

gaps.title: Function-field Mordell conjecture proofs
gaps.detail: Manin, Grauert (characteristic 0) and Samuel, Voloch (characteristic p) are cited through Poonen Theorem 9.5.10; not decomposed.

gaps.title: Unplanned scheme, curve and line-bundle supplier contracts
gaps.detail: The exact SchemeAndStackFoundations target references listed in requests do not exist in its current packet. SF.3–SF.5 have no target decomposition yet. The replacements are stage requests, not satisfied prerequisites. Required contracts include torsors/twists, regular Brauer comparison, Picard/curve geometry, Riemann–Roch/Riemann–Hurwitz, arbitrary-dimensional resolution, ample/very ample comparisons and intersection projection formulas. See the independently checked request list; scheme Brauer remains owned by key/scheme-brauer. The very-ample request also specifies generated-bundle difference presentations and their local coefficient bounds for the point-metric construction.

gaps.title: Lang–Néron proof contracts
gaps.detail: Conrad §7 pp.23–26 needs bounded-degree Hom/Albanese control and finite étale H¹ on a smooth curve. These are not supplied by the later height-kernel theorem, whose proof uses Lang–Néron; the previous circular route is removed.

gaps.title: Global-function-field adelic and cohomology extension
gaps.detail: RP.2 presently constructs number-field adelic points. The global-function-field theorems require an analogous integral-model direct limit and local topology, together with proper-torsor/finite-H¹ finiteness for prime-to-characteristic modules. Poonen §§8.4–8.6 verifies the assertions, but the lower-tier proof contracts remain unplanned; characteristic-dividing fppf finiteness is a further obligation.

gaps.title: Deep descent comparisons and universal torsor existence
gaps.detail: Poonen Thm.8.5.4 states the étale–Brauer/descent equivalence; its proof needs domination/composition of connected covers and the Demarche–Harari–Skorobogatov comparison, which is not decomposed. HW20 §6.1 invokes an external universal-torsor existence theorem for the rationally connected case; its book proof is unread. BGW descent-to-Brauer obstruction uses the Cassels–Tate/Brauer comparison, not merely empty Selmer sets.

gaps.title: Bombieri product and Roth lemma
gaps.detail: The statement of Bombieri §10 Thm.1–2 and the Mumford inequality were read and checked. The product/Roth lemma in §§6–9 is a deep proof input not decomposed by the present Vojta node; no complete no-gap Mordell proof can be certified until it is planned. The effective bound concerns high-point counts, not an effective bound on all heights.

gaps.title: Certified computation beyond compact local evaluation fibres
gaps.detail: Finite partitions follow from properness and local constancy. An algorithm additionally needs computable spreading, a finite exceptional set, terminating local solubility/evaluation tests and certified nonempty fibres. Those are requested from the computational roadmaps; the Iskovskikh calculation is only a worked special case.

gaps.title: Lefschetz, Brauer reciprocity and purity proof contracts
gaps.detail: The corrected proof sketches specify the required H²(μ_n)/Picard Lefschetz comparison, Brauer reciprocity on curves, and compactification/all-valuations purity. These are stage requests, not supplied by curve-only resolution, an intersection projection formula, or H³ of the base field.

gaps.title: Number-field S-adic Subspace Theorem adapter
gaps.detail: The full Corvaja–Zannier paper is now read. Its proof uses place-dependent linear forms over a general number field. DT.2 owns an absolute systems theorem, but the exact normalized product-form corollary used here must be supplied and linked; the previously cited rational-only product theorem is insufficient.

gaps.title: Formal lemma auxiliary-place proof
gaps.detail: HW20 uses the Colliot-Thélène–Skorobogatov formal lemma for finite A/(A∩Br X). Its statement and downstream use were read; the primary auxiliary-place proof is not decomposed here. Ramification, residue control and the existence of compensating local points are explicit proof obligations, not consequences of fixed-class local constancy alone.

gaps.title: Smooth-group formal-completion and local-chart interfaces
gaps.detail: The primary Mattuck and Katz statements and proofs have been read. The remaining implementation input is the exact general smooth formal-completion/kernel and p-adic identity-chart comparison requested from NeronModels R11.1. Its current elliptic formal-group comparison does not supply arbitrary dimension. The logarithm theorem, convergence radius and finite-group index count are planned here; this gap records the supplier interface, not an unread-source limitation.

sourceIssues.printed: The inclusion R→R′ is assumed to be a topological embedding, but the closed/open-subring condition is stated with the two ring names reversed.
sourceIssues.correction: Require R to be closed, respectively open, in R′; then X(R) is closed, respectively open, in X(R′). The inclusion is R→R′ throughout.
sourceIssues.reason: The embedding identifies R with a subring of R′. A finite affine presentation embeds X(R) into a power of R, whose image inside the corresponding power of R′ has the asserted closed/open property. The reversed condition is ill-typed for a proper subring. The subsequent discreteness comparison and the number-field, S-integer and local-integer examples use the correct inclusion direction.
